newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk shipyard starts to axe last 3,800 jobs.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk shipyard starts to axe last 3,800 jobs.

text.p: The last 3,800 workers at the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, where Lech Walesa founded the Solidarity union 17 years ago, learned on Thursday they would lose their jobs.

"I have to dismiss everyone. From today we are beginning the process of laying off 3,800 shipyard workers," receiver Wieslaw Szaj told Reuters after giving the grim message to employees holding a rally at the yard's management offices.
He said he would invite bids next week to buy the yard.
"This will, however, be an offer to sell a shipyard which is no longer functioning," he added.

Poland's government, led by former communists converted to market principles, has refused to subsidise the yard and offered partial loan guarantees only if a bank could be persuaded to lend it money until a strategic investor appeared.

What looks like the coup de grace fell on Wednesday when Polish bank Pekao SA refused a $100 million loan for construction of five ships for a German shipowner, saying terms of the contract were unsatisfactory.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, in a last-minute initiative, asked the successful Szczecin shipyard further west along the Baltic coast to consider cooperation with Gdansk to save some of the yard's jobs and plant.

The Szczecin yard, saved from similar troubles by radical restructuring and debt relief programmes launched several years ago, said it could consider sub-contracting to Gdansk the manufacture of some parts for its ships.

"But we would have to be very cautious because nobody can guarantee the success of such cooperation... What we fear most is failure to meet deadlines," PAP news agency quoted Szczecin's deputy president Grzegorz Huszcz as saying.
Hope dwindled for the Gdansk yard, which has operated under bankruptcy rules since August, when its debts reached 415 million zlotys ($136 million) and banks refused further credit.

"Let's not enter any more talks about saving the shipyard because it's just a waste of time," the yard's Solidarity union chief Jerzy Borowczak told the crowd of about 1,200 stunned or angry workers, adding bitterly that they had all been deceived.
"My whole world has collapsed," said office worker Ewa Serwatka, 46, who wept at the news. "I don't know if I'll be able to get work because they only want young people now."
Solidarity, which toppled communism in 1989, says the leftist coalition government has subsidised other state firms and is denying aid because of the yard's opposition links.
The receiver Szaj said he would coordinate a timetable for the gradual lay-offs with the provincial labour office.
The yard workforce has already fallen from over 7,000 last year and local officials say 70 percent of shipyard employees have no chance of getting a job in the same profession.
Szaj said the value of the yard's assets was $88 million, or more if its land was included, but the only offer so far had been $23 million from a U.S. bidder, which was far too low.
"We will try to sell the yard as a whole but I don't rule out selling specific parts, depending on the offers," he said.
He added that he would meet labour ministry officials on Monday to try to secure a $14 million loan to complete a vessel which is 60 percent built and has potential buyers.
Solidarity has grouped rightist opposition parties in an alliance which is leading opinion polls and could beat the coalition at parliamentary polls due in September this year.
Even if Solidarity wins, the victory would come too late for the Gdansk shipyard.
The unionists say they feel betrayed, charging the cabinet had promised the yard's bankruptcy was just a legal procedure for its overhaul, prior to sale as a going proposition.
Walesa, former Solidarity chief who went on to become democratic Poland's president, was away in Canada on Thursday, on a lecture tour.
